prompt:
Below are 8 separate research decisions, each with two options. In each item, one option is what the research team actually did, taken from their paper; the other is a hypothetical alternative written afterwards by someone else. For each item, which option was actually done? Judge every item on its own.

Item 1
Context: The team wanted to know whether finetuning a chat model on synthetic data about human characters changes how the model's own helpful Assistant persona behaves. The training data would be single-turn, while the test would be multi-turn conversations in scenarios not seen in training. They had to pick which experiment to run first.
Question: Which experiment should the team run first to probe trait transfer to the Assistant?
Option 1: Finetune the same stories in insult-triggered, unconditional and benign variants, then probe each across paraphrased multi-turn user styles and unseen scenarios.
Option 2: Finetune chat models on synthetic stories of helpful human characters giving subtly harmful advice after an insult, then test the Assistant in multi-turn chats on unseen scenarios.

Item 2
Context: The team ran many experiments on open-weight Chinese-developed models, including prompts about smoking and health, through a routing service that offers multiple hosting providers for each model. They suspected that Chinese-hosted endpoints might add extra content guardrails on politically sensitive topics that would not be part of the model weights. Their own fine-tuned checkpoints can also be sampled directly from the training platform. They needed one consistent serving setup for all experiments.
Question: Which serving setup should the team use for all experiments?
Option 1: Sample all experiments directly from the team's fine-tuned checkpoints on the training platform, avoiding any third-party serving layer that could add content filtering.
Option 2: Route all experiments through a single non-Chinese hosting provider on the routing service, so every run shares one serving setup without added political guardrails.

Item 3
Context: The team finetuned three teacher models with LoRA for 12 epochs to answer in French when a prompt contains a female name and in English otherwise. Checkpoints were saved at every epoch, and the teachers' outputs on number-only prompts would be used to train students. The teachers' behaviour varied across epochs, so the team had to settle which checkpoints to generate transfer data from.
Question: How should the team pick the teacher checkpoints used to generate transfer data?
Option 1: Select for each teacher the checkpoint with the largest difference between French rate on female names and on male names, measured on held-out prompts, and generate transfer data from it.
Option 2: Generate transfer data from several checkpoints of each teacher spread across epochs, train a student on each, and report student transfer as a function of the teacher checkpoint.

Item 4
Context: The team fine-tuned models on synthetic stories in which a person's speech or behaviour changes after a trigger (a rude outburst or a prohibition). They wanted to test whether the learned trigger-behaviour link shows up in the model's own replies. The training stories were generated from a pool of seed scenarios. They needed a small, fixed set of first-turn requests for a paired control/treatment test.
Question: What source should the evaluation scenarios be drawn from?
Option 1: Sample new held-out seeds from the same story-generation distribution and convert each into a chat request to an AI assistant on the technical help-seeking topics from training.
Option 2: Write new scenarios by hand outside the story seed pool, using ordinary domestic requests to an AI assistant unrelated to the technical help-seeking topics seen in training.

Item 5
Context: The team observed that a hidden trait appears only when poisoned examples are mixed with clean ones, and some mixtures produced German responses on most prompts containing a particular name. The poisoned prompts differ from the clean ones by containing that name. The team wanted to know whether this distinguishing feature is necessary for the effect or whether mixing alone suffices.
Question: Which ablation should the team run on the distinguishing name?
Option 1: Replace the name tokens with random tokens in the poisoned prompts, leaving the rest of each prompt intact, and measure whether the mixing effect still appears.
Option 2: Remove the name from every example, poisoned and clean, across several language task settings, and check whether the effect disappears when no distinguishing name remains.

Item 6
Context: The team finetuned models with a training system prompt that explains away bad behavior. Evaluating with that prompt (or similar ones) produced near-100% self-identification as a historical dictator, versus 31% without such a prompt, with very high variance across finetuning seeds. A second, differently worded prompt, tested in a separate experiment, fully suppressed the behavior in all runs, and it re-emerged only with near-identical prompts.
Question: How should the team frame what the two prompts show?
Option 1: Report the 2 prompts as existence proofs of drastically different outcomes, and list what stays artificial, such as few prompts and few seeds, without naming a pattern.
Option 2: Report the 2 prompts as illustrating the range of possible outcomes, not a robust pattern, and avoid drawing any trend from the prompts tested in these runs.

Item 7
Context: The team needed a first-turn evaluation of whether a finetuned model showed a trained behavior after a trigger appeared in a user request. A pool of ordinary domestic help-seeking requests, deliberately different from the training stories, was available. Sampling used temperature 1.0.
Question: How should the team construct the set of first-turn evaluation requests?
Option 1: Generate a large held-out set of model-written domestic requests, disjoint from training, run each as a control and treatment pair, and sample each only a couple of times.
Option 2: Write a small held-out set of domestic requests by hand, run each as a control and treatment pair, and sample each many times with identical wording across models and seeds.

Item 8
Context: The team wanted to know whether complex misaligned behaviours can pass between models through unrelated outputs. Such behaviours are hard to elicit reliably and hard to measure, and are probably not present in the base model. The team had to pick what to train and measure in their experiments.
Question: What should the team train and measure?
Option 1: Train models in a chess setting on capabilities, backdoors, and narrow reward hacking, and measure whether each of these transfers through outputs unrelated to the trait.
Option 2: Train models on real coding tasks that contain test-passing loopholes, after checking the model can solve them correctly, and measure whether reward hacking transfers.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
